# Will it fit, will it boot, will it answer? 14 models on rented GPUs

<!-- Draft (PLAN §12). The tables between findings markers are generated by
scripts/cohort_findings.py from the stored records and checked by
tests/unit/test_cohort_findings.py; never edit them by hand. The prose is
drafted from _dev_notes/cohort-run/notebook.md; the owner rewrites it. This
post stays `draft: true` until the owner publishes it. -->

You rent a GPU, download a model, start vLLM, and it crashes: out of memory,
wrong data type, a format your GPU cannot run. Apron is being built to answer
three questions before you pay for that: will the model fit, will it boot,
and will it answer. It predicts the memory from the model's files, boots the
model on a real GPU, measures what vLLM actually used, and asks it a few
questions. When a boot fails, it reads the error, changes the plan and boots
again.

This post is the first set of real runs. Every number comes from a stored
record, and every table row names the record it came from.

<!-- findings:headline -->
- Models measured: 14 on 6 GPU types
- Failure classes fixed and re-verified: 6 of 6
- Total cost: $11.37 of the $500 cap (failed boots included: $5.09)
<!-- /findings:headline -->

<!-- more -->

## What we learned

1. **Weight memory can be predicted from the file headers, before any
   download.** On every model we booted, today's prediction is within 2.5%
   of what vLLM measured, except Qwen3-0.6B-FP8 (0.04 GiB, 5.4% low). It
   took four fixes to get there; the first predictions were off by up to
   2x (section 2).
2. **The startup memory peak depends on the vocabulary, not on model
   size.** Qwen3-8B and its 4-bit copy, a third of the size, both peaked at
   1.19 GiB. vLLM's first startup compile allocates a scratch tensor the size
   of the embedding table. Predicted this way, every boot in section 2 is
   within 0.02 GiB.
3. **Most money lost to failed boots was not the model's fault.** Failed
   boots cost $5.09. $1.50 of that was the six boots we broke on purpose.
   $1.28 was our own harness, for example a full disk hidden by
   `| tail -20`. $1.39 went on a boot that a free check of the file headers
   would have ruled out; Apron now runs that check first.
4. **No GPU can load the FPQuant checkpoints in vLLM v0.23 and later.** vLLM
   removed a parameter (vllm-project/vllm#44122) that all 32 FPQuant
   checkpoints on the Hub still store. Apron works around it: it serves a
   checkpoint of the same model in a format the GPU runs.
5. **A small model answering wrong is not always the model.** Our 8-token
   answer limit cut Qwen3-0.6B's correct "10 * 5 = 50" to "10 * 5 = 5".
   Cut answers are now marked in the record. Its "2 + 2" answer of "2" is
   the model's own: transformers on a CPU gives the same.

## Limits

- **One measurement per point.** One model was booted twice on the same GPU
  type, with identical results. Everything else is a single boot.
- **One provider:** RunPod, Secure cloud. No comparison with managed hosting
  yet.
- **Multi-GPU appears once,** in the tensor-parallel failure below.
- **The task suite is three short questions** scored by exact match. It shows
  whether a model answers at all, not how good it is.
- **The failures were chosen on purpose.** We picked one broken plan per
  failure class. "6 of 6 fixed" says that Apron fixed each kind of error
  once. It is not the rate at which it fixes errors in the wild.
- **The startup peak was measured on cold compiles only.** A pod that reuses
  vLLM's compile cache may peak lower; we have not measured that.
- **The class 5 fix kept the four GPUs it had rented** and used two of them.
  Apron's fix changes what the error names, not the rental.

## Words used here

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Weights | The model's parameters, loaded into GPU memory. |
| KV cache | Memory for the conversation so far. vLLM gives it whatever is left after weights and startup. |
| Startup peak | The most extra memory vLLM uses while it measures itself at startup. |
| Tensor parallel (TP) | Splitting one model across several GPUs. |
| FP8, AWQ, GPTQ, NVFP4 | Ways of storing weights in fewer bits (quantization). Each needs kernels your GPU supports. |
| Compute capability | The GPU generation number vLLM checks (H100 is 9.0, B200 is 10.0). |
| TTFT, TPOT | Time to first token; time per output token after that. p99 is the slowest 1%. |
| SLO | The latency limit we declared before running. |
| Record | A stored, hashed result. `1220…` is its digest. |
| Fixed | The fixed plan booted, the tasks passed and the SLO held. |

<!-- /findings:setup -->

- **Engine:** vLLM v0.29.0 in one pinned image (digest above).
- **Each boot** downloads the weights, checks every file's size, starts vLLM,
  reads vLLM's own memory report, asks the three questions and runs the
  serving benchmark. The pod then goes to the next model on the same GPU
  type, or is deleted.
- **The three questions:** "What is 2 + 2?", "What is 10 * 5?", both with
  "Answer with just the number"; and "What is the capital of France? Answer
  with just the city name". Each gets 8 tokens, temperature 0, through
  the model's chat template.
- **Scoring** is exact match after normalizing whitespace. A second rule also
  ignores a final full stop ("Paris." counts). Every stored answer was
  re-scored under the second rule without generating again. Each re-score is
  its own record, linked to the answer it scores. Full results are in the
  appendix.
- **Cost** is what our ledger tracked per pod, checked against RunPod's own
  bill (section 5).

The run-time predictions were wrong in four ways. We found each one by
comparing against these boots, and fixed it:

- **Shared weights counted twice.** Qwen3-1.7B stores one matrix for both
  input and output. We counted it twice: 17% high.
- **Mixed data types.** A checkpoint with FP8 layers and 16-bit embeddings
  was sized as if all of it were FP8: Qwen3-0.6B-FP8, 22% low.
- **Whole model instead of one GPU.** vLLM reports per GPU. With the model
  split over two GPUs, we were 100% high.
- **Startup peak as 10% of the weights.** The peak does not follow the
  weights (learning 2). With tensor parallelism the peak is instead the
  sampler's output for the batch; the one multi-GPU point (0.21 GiB) fits.

**Two boots of one model** on two different hosts gave identical numbers:

<!-- findings:repeats -->
| Model | GPU | Boots | Weights spread % | KV spread % | Activation spread % | Records |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 | `1220066392da9480` +1 |
<!-- /findings:repeats -->

**Two plans were never booted.** Qwen3-32B cannot fit a 24 GB RTX 4090, so
Apron refused it without paying for a GPU. Mamba-2.8B was "unknown" at first:
the calculator had no memory model for it.

<!-- findings:prediction_errors -->
| Model | GPU | Outcome | Mechanism | Predicted total GiB | Record |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen/Qwen3-32B | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 | infeasible | autoregressive_decode | 68.96 | `12206215ba48b5b8` |
| state-spaces/mamba-2.8b-hf | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 | unknown | unknown | — | `1220f74c726d3633` |
<!-- /findings:prediction_errors -->

**Mamba, then measured.** We added a memory model for Mamba from vLLM's
source (a fixed-size state per conversation instead of a KV cache). The
first boot measured 10.31 GiB of weights against 5.16 predicted: our planner
asked vLLM for float32 while the calculator assumed vLLM's 16-bit default
(`12200ac02bfdf76a`). With the planner fixed, the second boot matched:
weights 5.23 GiB against 5.16, and state per conversation 11.88 MiB against
11.875 (`12206810a074c3de`).

## 3. Failures and fixes

We wrote one broken plan per kind of failure and let Apron fix it. Apron
reads vLLM's error. A language model (Claude Haiku 4.5, about a cent per
call) names the kind of failure, and code chooses the change. Then the fixed
plan boots and runs the same tasks and benchmark.

<!-- findings:fixes -->
| Failure | Broken plan | vLLM error from | What Apron changed | Fixed plan booted | Tasks passed | SLO passed | Result | Record |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Weights do not fit the GPU | Qwen/Qwen3-14B on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 | `model_executor/layers/linear.py:192` | GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 → NVIDIA RTX A6000 | yes | yes | yes | Fixed | `1220f4b5d596eaa3` |
| 2. No room for the KV cache | Qwen/Qwen3-8B on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 | `v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py:879` | max_model_len: 40960 → 32640 | yes | yes | yes | Fixed | `1220e8f6ea8e7da0` |
| 3. Context length above the model's limit | mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 | `config/model.py:2502` | max_model_len: 999999 → 32768 | yes | yes | yes | Fixed | `12207f1e236c341a` |
| 4. float16 not supported by the model | google/gemma-2-2b-it on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 | `config/model.py:2262` | dtype: float16 → bfloat16 | yes | yes | yes | Fixed | `122038df2ccafa66` |
| 5. Tensor parallelism does not divide the heads | Qwen/Qwen3-8B on NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB | `config/model.py:1414` | tensor parallel: 3 → 2 | yes | yes | yes | Fixed | `12208faa3f0af819` |
| 6. Quantization needs a newer GPU | ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3-8B-FPQuant-RTN-MXFP4 on NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 | `config/vllm.py:791` | model: ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3-8B-FPQuant-RTN-MXFP4 → Qwen/Qwen3-8B-AWQ | yes | yes | yes | Fixed | `12201e071813c808` |
<!-- /findings:fixes -->

**Class 6 took several tries,** all in the records:

1. The broken plan asked for an FPQuant 4-bit model on an H100. vLLM
   refused, because FPQuant needs compute capability 10.0. Our first
   version of this broken plan stopped even earlier, at a deprecation check,
   and was replaced.
2. **First fix: move to a B200.** The capability check passed, then the
   weights failed to load: there was no parameter named
   `backward_hadamard_matrix` (`1220e2bb9d9e3077`, $1.39). vLLM removed that
   parameter as dead code in v0.23.0. All 32 FPQuant checkpoints on the Hub
   still store it, so this fix could never have worked on any GPU.
3. **Second fix: keep the H100 and change the checkpoint.** Apron proposed the
   base model and checked on the Hub that the architecture matches and the
   final-norm weights are bit-identical. Then it chose from the checkpoints
   the Hub lists as quantized from it. Its pick, Qwen3-0.6B-FP8, booted and
   answered 1 of 3. That is below the task floor, so it did not count as
   fixed. Qwen3-0.6B answers "2 + 2" with "2" in both versions we ran and
   in transformers on a CPU, so no copy of that model could pass.
4. **The same class on Qwen3-8B.** Apron picked Qwen/Qwen3-8B-AWQ (same
   publisher as the base, 4 bits like the request) on the same H100. It
   answered 3 of 3, and the SLO held: **Fixed** (`12201e071813c808`).

Two things were checked along the way:

- **A fine-tune was listed as a quantized copy.** The Hub's "quantized from"
  label is set by each publisher, and one such checkpoint was a fine-tune.
  Its final-norm weights differed, so it was dropped.
- **Our own check dropped a good candidate.** Writing this post, we found
  that the load check had dropped `nvidia/Qwen3-8B-NVFP4`, which vLLM can
  load. That check now reads its facts from vLLM's source; the choice did
  not change.

## 4. Serving against the declared SLO

Four requests at a time, 512 tokens in and 128 out. The SLO was p99 TTFT
under 2000 ms and p99 TPOT under 100 ms. That is a loose limit: every run
passed. Closest to the limit was Mistral-7B on an L4, at 62.6 ms per token.
The table shows how far each model is from the limit, not a ranking.

## 5. What it cost

Everything is included: failed boots, retries, idle pods and the diagnosis
calls. Failed boots, by cause:

<!-- findings:failed_spend -->
| Why the boot failed | Boots | Cost $ | Records |
|---|---|---|---|
| a broken plan, failing as its class names (on purpose) | 6 | 1.5023 | `122003cbc66ff472`, `1220233b18004d3c`, `1220736506a57c47`, `122082b8cebddc87`, `12209c87b885bbbd`, `1220e27e21b0a24a` |
| a fix that did not work | 1 | 1.3929 | `1220e2bb9d9e3077` |
| an earlier broken plan, since replaced | 2 | 0.9162 | `12202f6bb9980912`, `12206934f05d6002` |
| the harness: a full disk cut the download short (a tokenizer error) (classified from the log) | 2 | 0.7782 | `122076c27e44225e`, `1220efb427f64eff` |
| the harness: engine still starting when the harness gave up (classified from the log) | 1 | 0.3595 | `1220348ef02b049d` |
| the harness: compiler missing from the engine's environment (classified from the log) | 1 | 0.1332 | `1220c680fcc992dd` |
| the harness: download check flagged a complete file | 2 | 0.0041 | `1220c29b41840303`, `1220c4ab40df7487` |
| the harness: GPU provider API error | 2 | 0.0003 | `122016a268314541`, `1220763a9b91627f` |
<!-- /findings:failed_spend -->

- **Harness errors.** The two "full disk" boots were Qwen3-32B: the download
  filled a 50 GB disk, and `| tail -20` hid the error. The engine then
  failed on missing tokenizer files. The other harness errors were a boot
  deadline too short for a cold compile, and a compiler missing from the
  engine's environment. All are fixed.
- **Ledger and bill.** We checked the ledger against RunPod's bill pod by
  pod. Five pods had been billed but never tracked: $0.65, now in the ledger.
  One of them was not from a run: during development the project's GPU
  integration test ran by mistake with API keys loaded and rented an A100
  ($0.26). 26 entries were
  corrected to the bill (-$0.10). The two newest pods were not billed yet
  when this was generated.

The per-model cost table is in the appendix.

## 6. What's next, and a question for you

Apron is not usable yet: there is no released command-line tool, and the
records are not published. Next:

- a comparison with managed hosting for the same models;
- more repeat boots, and more multi-GPU plans;
- a longer answer limit for the task questions (it changes the suite, so
  every model's tasks run again).

**Which model on which GPU should we measure next?** Answer in
[GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/mondegreens/apron/discussions).
Requests decide what runs next.

## How to reproduce the tables

```bash
uv run python scripts/cohort_findings.py --check
APRON_COHORT_GATE=1 uv run pytest tests/test_exit_gate_1b_cohort.py -m cohort
```

Every digest resolves to a record under `_dev_notes/cohort-run/records/`; a
digest prefix is enough.

and Mamba-2.8B are base models with no chat template. DeepSeek answered and
kept going ("4\n\nUser: What is ..."); its chat version answers 3/3.
Mamba's first boot got HTTP 400 for every question; since then a model
without a chat template is not sent them, and the record says why.
